title: The temple of his body (John 2:13–25)
hook: destroy this temple and in three days I'll raise it

segments.voice: Yesterday, the first sign at Cana, and the good wine kept until now. Your line: the best was kept till last.

Jesus in the temple, driving out the traders: Luke tells that scene at the end, in the last week. John puts it here, in chapter two, right at the start. Christians explain that in different ways. Some think it happened twice, once early and once late. Others think John placed it at the start on purpose, so it would frame the whole story. Either way, it's Passover, the city is full, and Jesus walks into the temple and finds it full of cattle, sheep, doves, and the tables of money changers.
screen: `LUKE PUTS IT LAST; JOHN PUTS IT FIRST.`

segments.voice: Some readers point out that the traders were serving pilgrims, who needed animals for the offerings. But Jesus makes a whip of small cords, drives out the sheep and oxen, pours out the coins, and turns over the tables. To the dove sellers he says: "Take these things hence; make not my Father's house an house of merchandise." My Father's house. The leaders ask him for a sign: what gives you the right? And he answers with a riddle: "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up." They hear it literally, and who wouldn't? "Forty and six years was this temple in building, and wilt thou rear it up in three days?" Then John tells us what the listeners missed: "But he spake of the temple of his body." For Israel, the temple was the place of God's presence among the people. John reads Jesus's riddle this way: that place is now a person, Jesus's own body. And even the disciples didn't get it at the time. Only after he was raised from the dead did they remember he'd said this, and believe. Christians later carried the idea one step further. Paul reminds the church in Corinth that "your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost which is in you." So for Paul the ordinary body, the one that gets tired and hungry and sore, is holy ground.
screen: then, large: `BUT HE SPAKE OF THE TEMPLE OF HIS BODY.`

segments.voice: Move your attention slowly up from your feet, legs, back, shoulders, hands, face, and notice where you're tired, tense or sore, without judging it. Then choose one kind thing for your body today, a glass of water, a walk, an early night, not to fix how you look but to honor where you live. If you pray, you can give thanks for your body.
Naos, the Greek word for the sanctuary, the inner house of God: what John says Jesus meant by destroy this temple, his own body, which would be raised in three days.
Your line: a temple of flesh. The place of God's presence, John says, became a person. Day five hundred ninety-eight, done.

howItsDone: Some lectionaries set John's account of the temple in Lent, and Paul's words that the body is a temple of the Holy Spirit shape Christian teaching about health, rest and the care of the body.

original.note: Greek: the sanctuary, the inner house of God. John uses it for 'this temple' in 2:19, not the word for the whole temple complex.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jesus lost his temper at the temple traders.
what it means: a sign that the meeting place of God and people is now a person, his body, destroyed and raised in three days.
what a scholar hears: John uses hieron for the temple courts and naos, sanctuary, for 'this temple'; and he places the scene at the start, unlike the Synoptics.

chat.says: When Jesus said destroy this temple and I'll raise it in three days, what did he mean?
options: John says he spake of the temple of his body, raised after three days.
He was promising to rebuild the stone temple himself if it was torn down.
He was warning the traders that the building would fall that same week.
chat.meaning: John says he spake of the temple of his body. Even the disciples understood only after he was raised from the dead.

Naos.meaning: Greek for a sanctuary, God's inner house

money changers.meaning: people who swapped coins for pilgrims at the temple

Paul.meaning: an early apostle whose letters are in the New Testament

Corinth.meaning: a Greek city whose church Paul wrote to

Holy Ghost.meaning: an older name for the Holy Spirit

notes: One cleansing or two: presented as 'some think twice; many scholars think John placed it early'. Confirm fairness.
Traders and money changers serving pilgrims (offerings, Tyrian shekels for the temple tax): common background. Confirm. The script avoids framing the temple or Judaism as corrupt.
